paragraphs: Hello, I'm Seth Simmons, and welcome to Season 1, Episode 8 of Opt Out. Opt Out's a show where I sit down with passionate people to learn why privacy matters to them, the tools and techniques they've found and leveraged, and where we encourage and inspire others towards personal privacy and data sovereignty. Wondering what alternatives are available for Twitter or similar centralized and censored services? This episode, we're sitting down with Sean O'Brien to chat about the need for decentralized and censorship-resistant microblogging and short messaging platforms.

Welcome to Opt Out, Sean. So glad we could finally get you on the show. I'm psyched to be here. Yeah, glad to be able to sit down and chat. You were one of the first guests that was recommended by a previous guest on Opt Out. Henry from Techlore sent me your name, and I was asking for people who would be a good fit. So I've seen some good work from you on Twitter, and just really excited to chat and hear your thoughts as kind of a professional in the security and privacy space, and see what your personal privacy journey has been through that.

But for my listeners who don't know much about you, would you mind just kind of introducing yourself? Sure. So I'm Sean O'Brien. I'm the founder of Privacy Lab, which is an initiative at Yale Law School. I also am the Chief Security Officer at Panquake, panquake.com, which we'll be talking about. And I've been working, you know, on and off on privacy and security-related projects for the better part of two decades. A big chunk of that has been on free and open source software.

I've done sysadmin work. I've done lots of digital self-defense workshops. And I get to do fun podcasts like this one. Awesome. Thanks. Yeah, I think a lot of the people that I've chatted with in Opt Out previously are kind of like getting into the space as a side thing. Like it wasn't their kind of initial career, that kind of thing. So it'll be cool to kind of talk through that. And I'm curious, what was it that woke you up to the need for personal privacy?

I mean, you've been in the space for a while, but what was it that kind of made that an important topic for you? Sure. So I think my experience being on the other side of technology, meaning the back end, you know, sort of secret world of technology, sort of opened my eyes to the potential for abuse. I think that was a big part of it. As the web sort of transitioned from the web I knew in the late 90s and early 2000s into something very different, something much more centralized, loading a lot of code from all over the place, but especially from entities we now call big tech.

As JavaScript became king and sort of broke down the client-server relationship in a way that was problematic for privacy and security as well in many cases. As a lot of code started getting injected into browsers without the user even being aware of it and executing. You know, working as a sysadmin and a web developer during that time and doing just other programming work, I just sort of felt that privacy was a really important frontier, if not the next big frontier that we needed to be pushing on from sort of a political sovereignty standpoint, actually.

I think it's really important for folks to think about their own lives, you know, self-sovereignty, I guess is what I'm really talking about. Think about their own lives within the context of the privacy they've given up, you know, in their technological transactions as well as, you know, potential, you know, future interactions. This is something now that's intermediating this technology we have that is very much not privacy respecting. It's now intermediating pretty much every aspect of life.

And there's just there's a huge amount of work to do. So, yeah, the writing started being on the wall for me, you know, during that time period when I was working on servers, basically. And I guess I should also say, you know, a lot of the credit for the things that I feel very strongly about it that was just sort of gestating in me comes from the free software movement, open source. You know, I think that's sort of digital rights movement from groups like the Electronic Frontier Foundation and so on.

I feel very strongly that free and open source software is exceedingly important for information to be free on the Internet, for freedom of speech, for, again, self-sovereignty, for people to have autonomy. And also, I think we've lost a lot of the digital commons that we used to have. So I guess if anything's gotten me into this battle, it is partially a longing for the Internet we used to have when I was growing up. Yeah, I love hearing that because I was, I mean, I'm a bit younger and kind of didn't get deeply into the Internet until I was in high school.

So I'm like pretty, pretty late to the game as far as seeing what the Internet used to be. So I always like getting in chat with people who kind of were involved, saw the kind of devolution of the Internet, the removal of the things that made it so powerful in the beginning or the change in the centralization. So it's good to hear from people like yourself on that topic. And I kind of echo a lot of the sentiments around why you got into privacy, because a lot of it came from working as a sysadmin, working in cybersecurity and seeing the tools and techniques that the other side can use.

And obviously, cybersecurity within a company, like it makes sense to surveil what's going on within your company to make sure that there's not obviously nefarious things going on, malicious actors, that kind of thing. But just seeing the toolkits that they have and the ways that they're able to surveil and building some of those out myself and learning those was definitely a key part of waking me up to why it matters that we take action rather than just hope for the best.

And what is it about privacy that makes it such an important topic for you today? I know that was a big driver for you early on and kind of why is it something that you're still focusing on today? Yeah. So at least since, of course, the Snowden disclosures and what we know about the security state now, you know, all the information that WikiLeaks has divulged and all the big leaks and hacks that we've seen in the last few years. We basically have open warfare on the Internet, right?

We have backdoors being built into operating systems, extremely polluted supply chains, both software and hardware. We have groups of both cyber criminals and state actors and sometimes, you know, working together, setting up botnets, breaking into systems, wreaking havoc across the world, really. And it has a real tangible effect on human beings. So I think as far as security and cybersecurity is concerned, I now is the time certainly to be very much vested in it, because if you're not paying attention, then you're just not paying attention to a big part of what's going on in the world right now.

From a privacy standpoint, I think it's interesting because we have more opportunities in some senses, you know, to have privacy respecting technology and cryptography that does really powerful things for us. And people are starting to use apps with end-to-end encryption and so on and so forth on a level that I had not hoped, right, five years ago, ten years ago, certainly. But we're also seeing a lot of doors being closed to us. We're seeing the information system being locked up, massive amounts of control of those information flows so people can't even find the things they want, you know.

And also, you know, basically misinformation from big tech, right, the apples of the world saying they love privacy and so on. And then you see what they're doing with photo scanning, right? Or I guess they took a step back. We'll remain to be seen if they follow through eventually. But the point being, I mean, that to me also is this thing we call privacy is really so firmly rooted in everything we do now that it really is about autonomy. And if you're not paying attention to that as an individual or as an organization, then you are potentially limiting yourself in very real ways as you move through the world.

Yeah, absolutely agree there. What's a common myth about personal privacy that you've run into? Probably the most common, and this comes up at almost every workshop, but also conversations like this very often, although I suspect you're much more astute and vested in privacy. But the big thing is the sort of don't, you know, they don't care about me-ism, right? Where people say, well, you know, nobody really cares about me, so why don't I just, you know, put all my stuff out there?

Yeah, that's probably the biggest one. Sometimes I call that, you know, privacy nihilism, but those two things are a little different. Folks also feel very disempowered, right? So even if folks are aware that they are being targeted or tracked and so on, they tend to feel that there's nothing they can do about it. So put together those two things are, I guess, a big myth. Yeah, I think those are two of the most common ones. I think the other one that most guests bring up is the kind of, I have nothing to hide, so why should I care?

I think that one ties in really closely to the first myth you talked about of, like, they're not watching me, so I don't need to worry about that. But I think people lose focus on the idea that dragnet surveillance is a very important thing. Like, you may not be targeted right now. Like, I doubt I am being surveilled in a targeted way right now, but that doesn't mean that dragnet surveillance isn't effective and that...

they're not collecting those things to potentially use them in the future when maybe they do target you and care about you. I think that's an important one. But yeah, definitely some myths that we hear quite often. What's a roadblock that you've seen people struggle with when it comes to personal privacy? I know those two are kind of similar. Often those are roadblocks to people. But is there any other that kind of stands out to you that prevents people from taking the jump into a personal privacy journey? Yeah. So I think the transactional view of privacy, right? The idea that we use technology just to get some specific job done. So install that app to talk to person X or my class requires me to install this crap on my computer. So I just got to install it just to do it.

Those kinds of roadblocks are very big and very real. And the entire privacy conversation, and I've been guilty of this in many instances as well, tends to veer towards this kind of view that there's sort of a consent based conversation going on, like a contract between you and the app developer or contract between you and the operating system maker or the gadget maker and so on and so forth. And I guess that that's sort of now has bled into the IoT world with everybody sticking ring doorbells on their front doors, Nest thermostats in their homes and Alexa speakers, etc, etc. So I think that sort of transactional concept is a real mental roadblock. It's very hard for us as humans to get past it. And in many ways, I think it's quite similar to some of our issues with other big problems, climate change and so on. It's just hard for us to do long term thinking in general. But also we're disincentivized from worrying about, you know, the future impacts of the choices we make today.

And how do you help motivate people to get past those roadblocks? Like how do you help them get past that transactional sense of privacy? So I try to, and this is getting easier, unfortunately, I try to use examples that are a little scary, right? So things that used to be confined to sci fi, which are starting to become very real, that are based upon someone's autonomy, their ability to move or have social mobilities or so on. So I'll talk about, for example, social credit systems, you know, Black Mirror, and other mostly Black Mirror, though, has really helped people understand that these things are possible and possible here in the United States. But also, you know, I'll talk about examples like, you know, a simple one would be self driving cars, right? Based upon what your app says you were doing, who you were with, whether you've paid your electrical bill, or your whatever your water bill, who the heck knows, it doesn't even have to be related, you know, somehow to technology.

You may literally not be able to get around cities if you have to hop in a self driving car and get home, right? You may be banned from these kinds of services the same way you can get banned now from subway systems in many parts of the world, because of facial recognition and other things like the payment scheme and so on. You know, those kinds of inability to move and ability to, of course, fly, we're seeing, of course, the TSA doing crackdowns and all kinds of things, and not just the TSA in the US, but other countries being pretty severely strict about flying, tying biometrics, right? So you're seeing that real sort of minority report reality coming. So using those examples and coming up hopefully with clever ones, a little more clever than I think I pulled from the top of my head. But talking about them, I think does scare people a little bit. And I'm not trying to, you know, I'm not trying to scare people just for the sake of scaring people or, you know, amplify their fear, so to speak. But I really just want to try to shock people into the moment.

You know, and these things are done, you know, not even necessarily in the most high tech ways, right? So car seats now are able to sense whether you're driving a car because of your weight, or the way that you angle your seat and so on and so forth. And profiles are being built on that stuff. Video cameras are, surveillance cameras are, you know, assessing people's gait in the way they walk. So even if they don't get your face, they're able to, you know, within a certain percentage, say that you're going somewhere.

Being able to stop people from living, working, moving, associating with each other, certainly assembling politically is a real serious reality. And, you know, as you said, whether or not you think you're being targeted directly, you know, that's, it's becoming more and more true that mass surveillance and targeted surveillance, there's less of a line between it. Targeted surveillance now can be scaled up so much. And the types of attacks that used to be reserved for specific, you know, quote unquote, risky individuals now are being used on large segments of the population, whether or not you're, you know, leaking documents or whatever.

Yeah, I think that point about the job of getting people past roadblocks is getting easier, unfortunately, is so true. I feel like especially in the last year, year and a half, I've seen so many people, I don't even need to convince them anymore. Like, I don't even need to, to explain some seemingly to them far off scenario of how, how a lack of privacy could hurt them, because they're seeing people hurt by a lack of privacy. I think it's, you know, privacy today in ways that they didn't even imagine. And I didn't imagine coming this quickly. But I think it's, it's been helpful to kind of shock some people awake kind of to show them, to show them reality and show them the potential use of today's surveillance in the future.

And I mean, even like you talked about the restricting of your ability to get around. I know in China, a really big deal is I think it's Alipay. I know they have a couple different ones. But if you can't use Alipay, or I think WePay is the other one, you can't get a taxi, you can't eat at most restaurants, you can't take the subway, you can't get a bus, like there's many systems you get locked out of just because you anger a specific big tech company, which obviously they're also working with the government in China.

But there are very many ways to do that. There aren't even a targeted thing necessarily, but just you upset the wrong person or do the wrong thing online or say the wrong thing in a group chat. And those things can happen quickly. And we don't think that they'll come here, like, for instance, to the US, but things can move a lot quicker than people expect. Yeah, and partially, you know, and I think this is very American, you know, these things are tied to incentive systems, right? You sign up for a GPS attached to your car because you want lower insurance rates, right? You, as the Wall Street Journal said today, the wallet's dead, right? They're talking about digital wallets and the system that Apple has and other digital sort of passport systems and so on.

Having all of your records on your phone while there's incentivization for that. There's obviously lots of people paying with apps because they get lower prices or freebies and so on. And these things are following them all around. When those things become, you know, compelled, and even if it's compelled in a small context, so to speak, so now you can't go around New York City or Boston, you know, it's still a really, really huge deal. And I suppose, you know, one of the things that one of the myths actually, which is not one of the common ones, which is worth talking about, is the flip side of the they don't care about me kind of thing where you have folks who just don't, you know, throw their caution to the wind.

There are a large number of folks, I think, in the privacy and security world, who still kind of believe that, you know, and, oh, well, you know, you can just get off grid and here's how you're going to do it. You know, and it's like, well, if you want to be completely ineffective and limited and go be a hermit in the woods and not interact with people, then you can get off grid, so to speak, and protect your privacy. But if we're talking about people being able to interact and work and live and go to school and also have political action, right, you know, build social movements and so on, then this idea that we should react to people who, oh, you're an idiot for using WhatsApp or you're an idiot, you know, that's just the wrong approach, you know, and kind of the myth of just being able to drop off the map, I think, is something that I actually combat, you know, I battle a bit.

And I suppose that's fueled by, you know, fiction as well, because there's always these hacker figures that can just kind of automatically drop off and no one can find them. And unfortunately, I don't think that's the world we live in. Yeah, I think that's a big thing I'm trying to combat with this show specifically is just that either that idea that like you can just completely disconnect or that you can, you can only gain privacy, or the only way to gain privacy is to do these insanely advanced, insanely difficult things.

Like there's no way to protect yourself unless you do all of these things that are just unattainable for the normal person. And it's something I've been trying to fight and just say like, yeah, maybe if you have a specific threat model, you need to get there. Like maybe if you are like targeted by multiple states, maybe you need to kind of figure out a way to disappear off the map. Or maybe that's something that fits your threat model. But for most people, they don't need to just disappear.

They need to find tools that can they can fit in and slot into the places in their life that they feel the need for privacy now and just slowly explore and expand their toolkit around that. But I mean, the other part of that is, you know,

resistant platforms for I know, like the language uses like micro blogging or short messaging, but just a way to be able to get thoughts out there that people can read without having to worry about widespread censorship.
